The question of whether a chicken can live without its head is genuinely contested. Several sources support the possibility under specific anatomical conditions: d1 (citing Dr. Wayne J. Kuenzel, a poultry physiologist at the University of Arkansas) explains that because a chicken's brain sits at a 45-degree angle in the skull, decapitation above the eyes can leave the cerebellum and brain stem intact, enabling basic motor functions and breathing. [d2] documents the most famous case, Miracle Mike, who survived for 18 months after decapitation on a Colorado farm in 1945. [d3] and [d4] (from Keele University and The Conversation) further explain that because a chicken's large eye sockets leave part of the brain residing in the top of the neck, a poorly aimed cut can leave enough brain tissue to sustain life. [d5] adds that survival is possible "for a short period of time" if the brain stem remains intact.

However, [d6] directly challenges this view: poultry expert Joyce Vaughn, with over 50 years of experience, states flatly, "When you cut their head off, the chickens will die," and the source argues that Mike was never truly headless because his brain remained intact despite the removal of most of his head. [d6] contends that "no creature can live without its head" and frames the Miracle Mike story as a case of misleading framing rather than genuine headless survival.

In summary, the evidence conflicts: [d1], [d2], [d3], and [d4] support that a chicken can survive decapitation under very specific circumstances (brain stem left intact), while [d6] argues this is a misconception and that true decapitation—removing the brain—is always fatal.
